Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has responded to rising prices by mulling a ban on US diesel producers selling overseas - a move which could push UK prices even higher. Crude oil is a key ingredient in petrol and diesel, which means that higher wholesale costs make filling up a car more expensive. items.text: The Gandhi Photograph You Carry In Your Wallet: Who Actually Took It And How Did It End Up On Indian Currency Notes?
items.article: This Gandhi Jayanti, look closely at your Rs 500 note. The famous face on your currency note wasn’t drawn Every day, over a billion people handle Indian currency notes featuring the smiling portrait of Mahatma Gandhi. Yet, despite its presence in almost every wallet across the nation, few know the origins of this iconic image. Contrary to common belief, the portrait is neither an artistic drawing nor an official state portrait. It is a cropped, mirrored section of an authentic photograph taken during a pivotal political meeting in Delhi in 1946. The original photograph was captured outside Viceregal House, now known as Rashtrapati Bhavan, in Delhi. Mahatma Gandhi was attending crucial political negotiations regarding the transfer of power alongside British diplomat Lord Frederick William Pethick-Lawrence. In the original full-length frame, Gandhi is seen standing next to Lord Pethick-Lawrence, sharing a candid, warm smile. The identity of the photographer remains disputed among historical archivists, though many attribute the historic shot to an unknown press photographer working for the British colonial administration. When the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) selected the image for currency design, security designers executed a subtle transformation. Designers cropped Lord Pethick-Lawrence out of the frame entirely, isolating Gandhi’s face and shoulders. items.article: One popular item could create serious problems once it ends up in household waste It can be easy to assume once something has gone in the bin , it is no longer your problem. But one binman has warned that a seemingly small and harmless item can create a much bigger headache for crews, councils and fire services. Ur Nans Favourite Binman shared the warning on TikTok after being asked what happens to discarded vapes and e-cigarettes. He said putting them in household bins is a "massive no-no" because devices containing batteries can create a fire risk when they are collected and processed. "Batteries, lithium batteries, toothbrushes, portable chargers and broken phones" were also among the items he urged people not to put in their bins. He said these products "need to be disposed of properly" because they can cause fires in bin lorries. The binman explained that a fire can have consequences far beyond the vehicle itself, potentially affecting residents, firefighters and the council responsible for the waste service. In his words, a lorry may have to be taken out of service and its entire load tipped out somewhere safe while crews deal with the situation. His warning is backed by official advice, with the Office for Product Safety and Standards telling people not to put vapes in general waste or household recycling.
